cards.front: Duplicated sister chromatids are held together by {{c1::cohesin}}, a protein ring that encircles DNA.
cards.quote: The sisters are held together by cohesin, a protein ring that encircles DNA.
cards.section: The picture: one duplicated chromosome, five phases

cards.front: What is a kinetochore, and where on a sister chromatid does it sit?
cards.back: A protein machine that grips spindle fibres. Each sister carries one at the centromere, so a sister pair has two kinetochores facing opposite ways.
cards.quote: At one constriction, the centromere, each sister carries a kinetochore, a protein machine that will grip spindle fibres.
cards.section: The picture: one duplicated chromosome, five phases

cards.front: Name the five phases of mitosis in a typical animal cell, in order.
cards.back: Prophase, prometaphase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase. The cell itself then splits in cytokinesis.
cards.quote: In a typical animal cell, mitosis has five named phases.
cards.section: The picture: one duplicated chromosome, five phases

cards.front: A diploid cell with 2n = 8 is in metaphase. How many chromosomes, chromatids and kinetochores does it have, and how many chromosomes does each daughter get?
cards.back: 8 chromosomes, 16 chromatids, 16 kinetochores; each daughter gets 8 chromosomes. Joined sisters count as one duplicated chromosome; after anaphase each sister counts as a chromosome.
cards.why: The DNA does not double at anaphase; only the counting rule changes.
cards.quote: While two sisters are joined, they count as one duplicated chromosome, even though each sister already has its own centromere and kinetochore.
cards.section: The picture: one duplicated chromosome, five phases

cards.front: State the three-part rule by which a mitotic cell gives each daughter one sister of every chromosome.
cards.back: Keep grips pulled from both sides (under tension), remake grips that are not, and cut cohesin only when no kinetochore is left empty.
cards.quote: Keep what is pulled from both sides, remake what is not, and cut only when no kinetochore is left empty.
cards.section: The picture: one duplicated chromosome, five phases

cards.front: A {{c1::k-fibre}} is the bundle of microtubules that connects one kinetochore to a spindle pole.
cards.quote: A k-fibre is the bundle of microtubules that connects one kinetochore to a pole.
cards.section: Grip: the spindle and the kinetochore

cards.front: In the search-and-capture model of spindle assembly, how are kinetochores captured, and why is that model alone not enough?
cards.back: Centrosomes fire microtubules in random directions until a plus end hits a kinetochore and is stabilized. Alone it would be slow, so cells also start microtubules near chromatin and kinetochores and as branches off existing ones.
cards.quote: Cells speed it up by also starting microtubules near chromatin and kinetochores and as branches off existing microtubules.
cards.section: Grip: the spindle and the kinetochore

cards.front: {{c1::Biorientation}} is the attachment in which each sister's kinetochore is attached to the opposite pole.
cards.back: The goal state for every sister pair.
cards.quote: Biorientation, the goal: each sister's kinetochore is attached to the opposite pole.
cards.section: Test and correct: how tension helps stabilize biorientation

cards.front: Syntelic and merotelic attachments are both errors. What distinguishes them?
cards.back: Syntelic: both sister kinetochores are attached to the same pole. Merotelic: a single kinetochore is bound by microtubules from both poles.
cards.quote: Merotelic: one kinetochore is bound by microtubules from both poles.
cards.section: Test and correct: how tension helps stabilize biorientation

cards.front: Why is a bioriented sister pair under tension while a syntelic pair, in the simple rope picture, is not?
cards.back: In biorientation one pole pulls each sister and cohesin resists, so the pair is stretched between its kinetochores. Same-direction pulls on a syntelic pair just drag it along.
cards.quote: A bioriented pair is the first case: one pole pulls each sister, cohesin resists, and the pair is under tension.
cards.section: Test and correct: how tension helps stabilize biorientation

cards.front: How does Aurora B kinase loosen a kinetochore's grip on microtubules when the attachment lacks tension?
cards.back: From its main site at the inner centromere, it phosphorylates outer-kinetochore proteins that grip microtubules, including the Ndc80 complex, weakening their grip so the attachment is released and remade.
cards.quote: It phosphorylates the outer-kinetochore proteins that grip microtubules, including the Ndc80 complex, and that weakens their grip.
cards.section: Test and correct: how tension helps stabilize biorientation

cards.front: In living vertebrate cells, Aurora kinase is blocked with a reversible inhibitor until wrong attachments pile up, then the inhibitor is washed out. What happens, and what does it show?
cards.back: The reactivated kinase selectively takes apart the wrong k-fibres and the chromosomes go on to biorient. Aurora activity corrects wrong attachments.
cards.quote: The reactivated kinase selectively took apart the wrong k-fibres, and the chromosomes went on to biorient.
cards.section: Test and correct: how tension helps stabilize biorientation

cards.front: Purified budding-yeast kinetochore particles are held on microtubules in a laser trap with no detectable Aurora B and no ATP. Pulling harder makes them stay attached longer. What does this show?
cards.back: Force stabilizes kinetochore-microtubule attachment directly, independent of Aurora B. In cells both mechanisms are thought to act together.
cards.why: The result does not show that Aurora B is unnecessary in cells.
cards.quote: In a laser trap, with no detectable Aurora B and no ATP, purified budding-yeast kinetochore particles stayed attached to microtubules longer when Akiyoshi and colleagues pulled harder.
cards.section: Test and correct: how tension helps stabilize biorientation

cards.front: Toy model: each of 46 duplicated chromosomes independently has a 1-in-2 chance of biorienting on the first try. How often would all 46 be right at once, and what does that imply?
cards.back: (1/2)^46 is about 1.4 x 10^-14, about 1 time in 70 trillion. First tries are unreliable, so error correction must give wrong grips another try.
cards.quote: all 46 would be right at once about 1 time in 70 trillion. Error correction gives wrong grips another try.
cards.section: Test and correct: how tension helps stabilize biorientation

cards.front: Does tension between sister kinetochores prove that a pair is correctly attached?
cards.back: No. Tension is a strong sign, not proof. Real syntelic and monotelic attachments can bear load from pushes on the chromosome arms and other forces.
cards.quote: so biorientation is the usual source of opposed sister tension, not the only way to load a grip.
cards.section: Test and correct: how tension helps stabilize biorientation

cards.front: Trace how a wrong grip ends up delaying anaphase through the spindle-assembly checkpoint.
cards.back: Wrong grip, little tension, Aurora B turns it over, kinetochore empty, wait. The empty kinetochore sends a wait-anaphase signal that holds back APC/C-Cdc20.
cards.quote: An empty kinetochore sends the wait-anaphase signal of the spindle-assembly checkpoint, which holds back the APC/C-Cdc20
cards.section: Test and correct: how tension helps stabilize biorientation

cards.front: A kinetochore has only side-on contacts with microtubules and is under some tension. Does it still send the checkpoint's wait signal?
cards.back: Yes. Only enough end-on attachment silences a kinetochore, whether right or wrong; side-on contacts are not enough, even under tension.
cards.quote: A kinetochore with enough end-on attachment stops sending it, whether its attachment is right or wrong; side-on contacts are not enough.
cards.section: Test and correct: how tension helps stabilize biorientation

cards.front: A PtK1 cell is stuck before anaphase with one chromosome attached to only one pole. A laser destroys that chromosome's unattached kinetochore. What happens, and what does it show?
cards.back: About 20 minutes later the cell enters anaphase, though the damaged chromosome never aligns. The wait signal comes from in or near the unattached kinetochore, not from failed alignment.
cards.why: Destroying an attached kinetochore while another chromosome stayed unattached did not release the delay.
cards.quote: About 20 minutes later the cell entered anaphase and pulled its chromosomes apart.

cards.front: A human cell has 45 bioriented chromosomes and one monotelic pair (one sister attached, the other free). Does it enter anaphase?
cards.back: No. The free kinetochore is empty, and any empty kinetochore means wait, even 1 out of 92.
cards.quote: The checkpoint's logic is the opposite: any empty kinetochore means wait, as one did in Rieder's cell.
cards.section: Wait: the checkpoint reads emptiness

cards.front: In a toy model with random, independent attachment times, why is a sensor for the last empty kinetochore better than a timer?
cards.back: The last attachment comes at about 4.4 tau on average; a timer at that average would fire with an empty kinetochore in about 43% of cells, and needs about 8.4 tau for 99% safety.
cards.quote: In this model, waiting for the last kinetochore is both faster and safer.
cards.section: Wait: the checkpoint reads emptiness

cards.front: Does the spindle-assembly checkpoint read chromosome alignment at the metaphase plate?
cards.back: No. Alignment normally accompanies biorientation, but it is a symptom, not the signal; the checkpoint reads empty kinetochores.
cards.quote: Rieder's damaged chromosome never aligned, yet anaphase followed.
cards.section: Wait: the checkpoint reads emptiness

cards.front: What kind of enzyme is the APC/C, and which two key targets does APC/C-Cdc20 tag at anaphase?
cards.back: An E3 ubiquitin ligase. With Cdc20 it tags securin and cyclin B for destruction by the proteasome.
cards.quote: APC/C bound to its coactivator Cdc20 tags two key targets.
cards.section: Cut: securin, separase and cohesin

cards.front: Before anaphase, {{c1::securin}} binds separase and keeps it inactive.
cards.back: Its destruction after APC/C-Cdc20 tagging releases separase.
cards.quote: Securin binds separase and keeps it inactive.
cards.section: Cut: securin, separase and cohesin

cards.front: Separase, a cysteine protease, cuts the kleisin subunit of cohesin, {{c1::Scc1}} (Rad21 in vertebrates), and the ring opens.
cards.quote: It cuts the kleisin subunit of cohesin, Scc1 (called Rad21 in vertebrates), and the ring opens.
cards.section: Cut: securin, separase and cohesin

cards.front: What two effects does destruction of cyclin B at anaphase have in a vertebrate cell?
cards.back: It inactivates CDK1, which lets the cell leave mitosis, and it lifts a second brake on separase, because CDK1-cyclin B inhibits separase in vertebrates.
cards.quote: Its destruction inactivates CDK1, which lets the cell leave mitosis.
cards.section: Cut: securin, separase and cohesin

cards.front: Budding yeast are arrested at metaphase with separase held inactive, and Scc1 is then made to be cleaved. The sisters separate and segregate. What does this establish?
cards.back: Cleaving Scc1 is sufficient to separate sisters. A sufficiency test is stronger evidence than watching a protein vanish at anaphase.
cards.quote: That sufficiency test is stronger than watching a protein vanish.
cards.section: Cut: securin, separase and cohesin

cards.front: Why is the separation of sister chromatids at anaphase a one-way step?
cards.back: A cut cohesin ring cannot be rejoined, and in a normal cycle sister cohesion is set up only during replication, so the next S phase pairs new sisters.
cards.quote: A cut cohesin ring cannot be rejoined.
cards.section: Cut: securin, separase and cohesin

cards.front: A human cell with every kinetochore attached and a silent checkpoint is treated with a proteasome inhibitor. Securin is ubiquitylated normally. Predict what happens to the sisters.
cards.back: They stay joined. If securin is tagged but cannot be degraded, separase stays inactive and centromeric cohesin is not cut.
cards.why: The APC/C and the proteasome together destroy securin; separase only cuts cohesin once securin is gone.
cards.quote: Keep the division of labour straight: the APC/C and the proteasome destroy securin; separase cuts cohesin.
cards.section: Cut: securin, separase and cohesin

cards.front: A vertebrate cell expresses a cyclin B that the APC/C cannot destroy, while securin is destroyed normally. Predict two consequences.
cards.back: CDK1 stays active, so the cell cannot leave mitosis; and CDK1-cyclin B keeps a second brake on separase, so cohesin cutting may be impaired.
cards.why: Rests on two stated rules: cyclin B loss inactivates CDK1 to exit mitosis, and in vertebrates CDK1-cyclin B inhibits separase.
cards.quote: In vertebrates it also removes a second brake on separase, because CDK1-cyclin B inhibits separase there.
cards.section: Cut: securin, separase and cohesin

cards.front: In vertebrates, why does the separase cut at anaphase act mainly at the centromere?
cards.back: Most arm cohesin leaves earlier, in prophase and prometaphase, without a cut, by the prophase pathway; shugoshin protects centromeric cohesin until separase cuts it.
cards.why: In budding yeast, by contrast, most cohesin is cleaved at anaphase.
cards.quote: During prophase and prometaphase most arm cohesin leaves without a cut, by a phosphorylation route called the prophase pathway.
cards.section: Cut: securin, separase and cohesin

cards.front: In human cells, SA2 phosphorylation is essential for the prophase pathway, and shugoshin depletion causes early loss of centromeric cohesin. Propose how shugoshin protects centromeric cohesin.
cards.back: Their results suggested it works by preventing SA2 phosphorylation at centromeres, so the prophase pathway cannot remove cohesin there; it stays until separase cuts it.
cards.quote: phosphorylation of the cohesin subunit SA2 was essential for the prophase pathway
cards.section: Cohesin removal in vertebrate prophase

cards.front: What moves in anaphase A, and what moves in anaphase B?
cards.back: Anaphase A: chromosomes move toward their poles, so each kinetochore-to-pole distance shrinks. Anaphase B: the poles themselves move apart.
cards.quote: In anaphase A the chromosomes move toward their poles: each kinetochore-to-pole distance shrinks.
cards.section: Move: anaphase A and B, read from a movie

cards.front: In many animal cells, what drives anaphase B?
cards.back: Motors slide apart overlapping microtubules in the spindle midzone, and dynein at the cell cortex pulls on astral microtubules.
cards.quote: motors slide apart the overlapping microtubules in the spindle midzone, and dynein at the cell cortex pulls on astral microtubules
cards.section: Move: anaphase A and B, read from a movie

cards.front: In cultured mammalian cells, a mark is bleached on kinetochore microtubules, and the chromosomes move toward the mark. Where do the k-fibres mainly lose subunits?
cards.back: Mainly at the kinetochore, though a small loss elsewhere was not excluded. If subunits were lost mainly at the poles (poleward flux), the mark would move toward the pole instead.
cards.why: In some other cells, such as Drosophila embryos, poleward flux contributes much more.
cards.quote: bleached a mark on kinetochore microtubules in cultured mammalian cells and found that the chromosomes moved toward the mark
cards.section: Where k-fibres lose subunits

cards.front: In a time-lapse of a mammalian cell (straight spindle, steady movement), at anaphase onset the poles are 10.0 um apart and each kinetochore is 4.0 um from its pole. After 5.0 min the poles are 14.0 um apart and each kinetochore is 1.5 um from its pole. Find the anaphase A and anaphase B rates.
cards.back: Anaphase A = (4.0 - 1.5) / 5.0 = 0.5 um/min. Anaphase B = (14.0 - 10.0) / 5.0 = 0.8 um/min of pole separation.
cards.quote: Kinetochore-to-pole distance fell from 5.5 to 1.5 um in 4.0 min.
cards.section: Worked problem: two rates from one movie

cards.front: Same movie: poles 10.0 to 14.0 um apart and each kinetochore 4.0 to 1.5 um from its pole over 5.0 min. How fast do the sisters separate?
cards.back: Separation = pole distance minus both kinetochore-to-pole distances: 10.0 - 8.0 = 2.0 um, then 14.0 - 3.0 = 11.0 um. Rate = 9.0 / 5.0 = 1.8 um/min, which equals 2(0.5) + 0.8.
cards.quote: The distance between sisters is the pole distance minus both kinetochore-to-pole distances.
cards.section: Worked problem: two rates from one movie

cards.front: A movie tracks only chromosomes, and sisters separate at 3.0 um/min. Can you find the anaphase A rate?
cards.back: No. Sister separation = 2 x anaphase A + anaphase B, one equation with two unknowns. You also need the pole positions.
cards.quote: A movie that tracks only chromosomes cannot tell you how much of their separation came from the poles.
cards.section: Worked problem: two rates from one movie

cards.front: Why can a merotelic kinetochore escape both the spindle-assembly checkpoint and Aurora B correction?
cards.back: The kinetochore is attached, so it sends no wait signal; and the pair is partly under tension, so Aurora B can miss it. The cell enters anaphase with the error in place.
cards.quote: The checkpoint does not: the kinetochore is attached, so it sends no wait signal.
cards.section: The rule's blind spot: merotely, laggards and micronuclei

cards.front: In PtK1 cells, lagging single chromatids appear in 1.16% of untreated anaphases and 17.55% after recovery from a nocodazole block, and electron microscopy shows microtubules from both poles on lagging kinetochores. What does this show?
cards.back: Merotelic attachment causes lagging chromatids: the kinetochore is pulled toward both poles at once in anaphase, and nocodazole recovery raises merotely.
cards.quote: Lagging single chromatids appeared in 1.16% of untreated anaphases and 17.55% after recovery from a nocodazole block
cards.section: The rule's blind spot: merotely, laggards and micronuclei

cards.front: What two fates can a lagging chromosome in anaphase have?
cards.back: It can reach the main nucleus late, or end up in a micronucleus, a small separate nucleus. In RPE1 and U2OS cells most transient laggards rejoined the main nucleus.
cards.quote: It can reach the main nucleus late or end up in a micronucleus, a small separate nucleus.
cards.section: The rule's blind spot: merotely, laggards and micronuclei

cards.front: In RPE1 cells, 9% of cells had at least one transient laggard, and 6% of lagging chromosomes formed micronuclei. Assuming one laggard per affected cell, what fraction of all cells has a laggard-derived micronucleus?
cards.back: 0.09 x 0.06 = 0.0054, about 0.5%. The 9% is per cell and the 6% is per chromosome.
cards.quote: If every affected cell had exactly one laggard, the fraction of all cells with a laggard-derived micronucleus would be 0.09 x 0.06 = 0.0054, about 0.5%.
cards.section: The rule's blind spot: merotely, laggards and micronuclei

cards.front: Multiplying a per-cell laggard frequency by a per-chromosome micronucleus frequency assumes one laggard per cell. If some cells have several laggards, which way could the true per-cell micronucleus fraction move?
cards.back: Either way: higher if extra laggards are independent, lower if micronuclei cluster in a few cells with many laggards. State the assumption whenever denominators differ.
cards.quote: Say the assumption out loud whenever you multiply rates with different denominators.
cards.section: The rule's blind spot: merotely, laggards and micronuclei

cards.front: Destroying the last unattached kinetochore in PtK1 cells releases anaphase; pulling a mono-oriented chromosome with a microneedle in mantis spermatocytes also ends the delay. Do these contradict each other on whether the checkpoint reads attachment or tension?
cards.back: Not necessarily. Tension stabilizes attachment, so pulling can change how many microtubules stay bound as well as the force. Attachment and tension are coupled.
cards.why: The two papers also used different systems (meiosis vs mitosis), so differences may reflect the cell.
cards.quote: Tension stabilizes attachment, so in a cell, pulling on a kinetochore can change how many microtubules stay bound as well as the force.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Design an experiment in cells to test whether anaphase delay comes from unattached kinetochores or from lack of tension. Include the readout and a control.
cards.back: Change one variable while holding the other fixed: ablate the last unattached kinetochore vs a cell whose kinetochore is attached but under low tension (drug dampening spindle forces). Readout: time to anaphase onset. Control: irradiate an equal spot off the kinetochore.
cards.quote: To separate them, change one while holding the other fixed.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: How does augmin generate new spindle microtubules?
cards.back: It recruits gamma-TuRC, the template that starts microtubules, onto the side of an existing microtubule, so a new one branches off in the same direction.
cards.quote: Augmin is a protein complex that recruits the gamma-tubulin ring complex (gamma-TuRC), the template that starts new microtubules, onto the side of an existing one
cards.section: Where spindle microtubules come from

cards.front: CENP-E, a kinetochore kinesin, is inhibited in human RPE1 cells early in prometaphase. Predict the effect on attachments and on the timing of anaphase.
cards.back: Side-on contacts are converted to end-on attachments less well; since side-on contacts do not silence a kinetochore, the checkpoint should keep delaying anaphase.
cards.why: Combines the CENP-E result with the rule that only enough end-on attachment stops the wait signal.
cards.quote: Inhibiting CENP-E, a kinetochore kinesin (see molecular motors), impeded the conversion of side-on contacts into end-on attachments.
cards.section: Where spindle microtubules come from
